why: The only linked/cloned repository is aappleby/smhasher, which is the upstream C++ MurmurHash + hash-testing suite the paper cites as its hash primitive. It contains no Bloom filter, no Rational Bloom filter, no Variably-Sized Block Bloom filter, no Figure 6 experiment driver and no data-generation scripts. There is therefore no author entrypoint that produces C1 or C2, and nothing to run 'as released'. The claims are, however, small and fully specified (m=8192, n=1000, k*=5.678, 10,000 non-inserted queries, MurmurHash + double hashing), so they can be reimplemented directly from the paper's description with a Python Bloom filter plus an mmh3/pure-Python MurmurHash3-64 primitive. Missing code is cheap to rebuild, so a faithful reimplementation of the C1 inequality (with C2 as a free cross-check) is the right plan.
missing_artifacts: Rational Bloom filter (floor(k) hashes + one hash activated with probability frac(k)) implementation
Standard Bloom filter baseline used in Figure 6
Variably-Sized Block Bloom filter implementation (needed only for the secondary figure, not for C1)
Figure 6 experiment driver (k sweep, m/n settings, 10,000-query FPR measurement)
Data generator for the synthetic insertion / disjoint query sets (paper gives the recipe only)
Any author config or seed list tying the runs to the reported curve
blockers_seen: The linked repository is a hash-function test suite (C++, CMake), not the paper's Bloom filter code; running it produces hash benchmarks, not FPR numbers
No Python code in the repo (n_python=0) and no dependency files, so nothing in it is importable for a Python reproduction
Paper reports no exact FPR value for the Figure 6 top point, so only the Theorem-1 inequality (RBF_FPR - BF_FPR <= 0) can be targeted, not a numeric FPR
No GPU on this machine (irrelevant here: the whole experiment is a few million hash computations)

feasibility.est_runtime_on_this_machine: Under 1 minute of pure-Python compute for the C1 point (1,000 insertions + 10,000 queries at k~6); a few minutes if the full Figure 6 k-sweep at both m/n settings is included, plus ~1 minute to install mmh3 (or 0 if MurmurHash3 is implemented in-repo).

compute.basis: Two 8-16 kbit Python bitsets, 1,000 insertions and 10,000 queries with ~6 double-hashed probes each (about 66k hash evaluations), repeated over ~10 seeds plus a small k-sweep for the C2 cross-check; the cost is dominated by writing and validating the reimplementation, not by the runs.
